rows: Employers must manage ionising-radiation risks to workers and the public.
Radiation work should be risk assessed before exposure occurs.
Depending on risk, work may require notification, registration or consent.
Exposure should be restricted as low as reasonably practicable.
Engineering controls and design features should be prioritised.
Suitable systems of work, controlled areas and supervision may be required.
Dose monitoring, assessment and records are required where applicable.
Specified radiation incidents must be reported through the appropriate route.
Possession of an X-ray or radioactive source does not establish a person's radiation dose.
Dose conclusions require source, activity, geometry, shielding, time, monitoring, controls and incident evidence.
Optical radiation includes ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation.
Employers should identify hazardous optical-radiation sources.
Risk from hazardous artificial optical radiation should be reduced as low as reasonably practicable.
High-power lasers can cause serious eye injury and skin burns.
Ultraviolet radiation can damage eyes and skin.
Enclosure, interlocks, screening and controlled access can reduce exposure.
Workers need information and training appropriate to the source.
Controls should be reviewed after equipment, process or exposure changes.
A laser class label or UV forecast does not establish actual occupational exposure.
Exposure conclusions require wavelength, power, beam path, duration, distance, controls, PPE and user behaviour.
People manufacturing or storing explosives must take measures to prevent fire and explosion.
Controls should limit the extent and spread of a fire or explosion.
People must be protected from the effects of an explosive event.
Storage may require licensing and applicable separation distances.
Explosives should be stored in suitable places and conditions.
Manufacture, transfer, record keeping and disposal have specific regulatory controls.
Discarding and decontaminating explosive-contaminated items must be performed safely.
Emergency and security arrangements should reflect the type and quantity of explosives.
A licence or inventory entry does not prove that current storage and operations are safe.
Site conclusions require explosive type, hazard category, quantity, store, separation, security, operations and emergency evidence.
Confirmed mpox cases can require structured contact tracing.
Contacts should be risk assessed according to the nature and circumstances of exposure.
Contact categories support proportionate public-health advice and follow-up.
Assessment should consider direct physical contact and contaminated materials.
Some contacts may need symptom monitoring or restrictions.
Vaccination advice depends on current eligibility and exposure guidance.
Cases and contacts should receive clear information about reducing onward transmission.
Public-health guidance should be updated as evidence and circulating clades change.
A venue attendance or contact list does not prove transmission or infection.
Individual conclusions require case confirmation, exposure type, timing, symptoms, vaccination and public-health assessment.
